transcript.content: Hello, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Yeah, um… I guess the reason I’m here is that I haven’t been able to let go of something that’s been going on for almost two years now. It started after this commission I had—professionally, I’m a music director and composer, so commissions are a pretty big deal for me—and after that, I became certain that a few people in the ensemble were… not openly attacking me, exactly, but quietly trying to undermine my work.

It’s been things like schedule changes that don’t make sense, or seating choices that affect how the piece comes across, or little comments in rehearsal that sound casual if you write them down, but in the room they feel pointed. And I know people have shown me emails or rehearsal notes that supposedly explain why something happened, but I still can’t shake the feeling—well, more than a feeling—that those explanations are covering for something else.

I’ve tried to talk myself out of it, and I know on the surface some of it can look like normal ensemble logistics, but it keeps lining up in a way that feels too specific to be accidental. That’s really what’s brought me in.
Do you believe it is definitely true that these people are deliberately trying to undermine you?

Yes. I mean… I know “definitely” is a strong word, and I know that’s probably the word you’re listening for, but yes, that’s how it feels to me. It’s not just a vague insecurity or me being sensitive after a stressful project. It’s been almost two years of the same pattern.

After that commission, there were certain people in the ensemble where things just started happening around my work—schedule changes that seemed to disadvantage the piece, seating decisions that changed how the sound carried, little rehearsal comments that could be dismissed as harmless but landed very specifically. And when I’d ask about it, there’d be an email or a note or some explanation ready, like, “Oh, this was just logistics,” or “This was decided earlier,” but it never really answered the bigger thing for me.

So yes, I believe they were deliberately trying to undermine me. I’ve tried to talk myself out of it, because I understand how it sounds if you isolate each incident, but taken together it feels too coordinated to be accidental.
Have you heard voices when no one else was there?

No, I don’t think so. I mean, I’ve replayed conversations in my head a lot—probably too much—but that’s different. It’s more like remembering exactly how someone said something in rehearsal and going over the tone of it, or thinking through what I should have said.

But hearing an actual voice when nobody is there, like outside my head or as if someone is speaking in the room? No, I haven’t noticed anything like that.
Even before this commission happened, did you generally find it hard to trust other people’s motives?

I’m not sure. I mean, I don’t think I walked around assuming everyone had bad motives, if that’s what you mean. Before the commission, I could be cautious, maybe a little analytical about people—especially in professional settings, because music work can be competitive and people can be subtle about status or credit or influence. So I’d notice tone, politics, who gets asked back, that kind of thing.

But I wouldn’t have described myself as unable to trust people generally. I had collaborators I trusted, and I don’t think I was constantly suspicious in every situation. It’s more that after this particular project, with those particular people, everything started to feel like it had this pattern to it. Before that, I guess I was careful, maybe sometimes overly careful, but not like this.
Has any part of this felt impossible in an ordinary way—for example, that they were influencing you or your work through special technology, hidden signals, or something supernatural?

No, not like supernatural or special technology. I don’t think they were, you know, transmitting things into my head or using hidden signals in some impossible way. It’s not that.

What I mean is much more ordinary, which is partly why it’s been so hard to explain without sounding like I’m making too much of small things. It’s things like schedule changes after the commission that put my work at a disadvantage, or seating choices that changed how the sound carried, or little comments in rehearsals that sounded casual but felt pointed, like they were meant to shape how other people saw the piece.

And then when I asked about it, there would always be some email or note or explanation ready—“this was logistics,” “this was decided earlier,” that kind of thing. So it’s not impossible in the sense of technology or anything supernatural. It’s that I can’t shake the certainty that a few people were quietly, deliberately undermining me in ways that could always be explained away afterward.
Since this started, have you become much less interested in seeing people or doing your work than you used to be?

Not really, no. I mean, I’ve probably been more preoccupied with the ensemble situation than I’d like, and it can take up space in my head, but I wouldn’t say I’ve stopped functioning or lost interest in everything.

Outside of that issue, I’m still doing my work. I meet deadlines, I keep composing, I’m still able to sit down and actually write. Sometimes it takes me longer to settle because I’m thinking about what happened, but I do get it done. And I still run most mornings, which is kind of how I clear my head—if I stopped doing that, I think my wife would notice immediately.

At home things are basically steady. My wife and I are okay. I’m not withdrawing from her or just lying around doing nothing. I guess I’m less eager to see certain music people connected to all of this, but in general, no, I wouldn’t say I’ve become much less interested in people or my work overall.
Apart from the people involved in that ensemble, have you also become convinced that other people are trying to harm or undermine you?

No, not really outside of them. I don’t think strangers are after me or that everyone in the field is part of it. It’s much more specific than that.

It’s those few people around the commission and the ensemble. That’s what I keep coming back to. For almost two years now I haven’t been able to shake the feeling—well, not just a feeling, really—that after that commission, certain things started happening in a pattern: schedule changes that made my work harder to present properly, seating choices that affected how the piece came across, little comments in rehearsal that sounded harmless but seemed aimed at making people doubt the work or doubt me.

And I know how it sounds, because each individual thing can be explained. They’ll show an email or say, “No, that was decided for logistics,” or “That wasn’t about you,” or “That note was just about balance.” But taken together, it doesn’t feel accidental. It feels deliberate, just done in a way that’s easy to deny.

So, no, I wouldn’t say I’m convinced other people in general are trying to harm me. It’s this specific group, this specific situation, that I can’t let go of.
Has anyone told you that your speech or thinking has seemed disorganized or hard to follow?

No, I don’t think so. At least no one has said that to me directly.

I can be long-winded, I know that. My wife has told me I explain things like I’m building a legal case, where I have to include every little piece so the other person understands why I’m saying what I’m saying. And in rehearsals or meetings, I’m probably more detailed than some people want. But that’s different from being hard to follow, I think.

I mean, people may disagree with my conclusions, or they may think I’m reading too much into certain things, but I don’t think anyone has said my actual speech is incoherent or that I jump around in a way that doesn’t make sense. If anything, I probably over-organize what I’m saying. I go back and explain the context, then the sequence, then why it matters. So, no—not that I’ve noticed.
If someone you trust showed you clear proof that these ensemble members were not trying to undermine you, would you be able to accept that?

I’d like to say yes, because I don’t want to be unreasonable. If someone I really trusted sat me down and showed me something clear, I would look at it. I’m not trying to ignore evidence just for the sake of it.

But honestly… I don’t know that an email or a note would fully settle it for me, because that’s kind of been the problem already. People have shown me explanations—emails about scheduling, notes about seating, rehearsal comments framed as normal musical direction—and on paper each one can look innocent. I understand that. I can follow the “official” explanation.

It’s the pattern that I can’t get past. After that commission, it felt like a few people in the ensemble started doing things in these small, deniable ways that affected how my work came across. A schedule change here, a seating choice there, a little comment in rehearsal that plants doubt without openly saying anything. So if someone showed me one clean explanation, part of me would still wonder whether that was just the part that could be documented.

So… could I accept it? Maybe if it explained the whole pattern, not just one piece of it. But I have to be honest, it would be hard for me to just drop the certainty I’ve had about this for almost two years.
Do you believe this is something you could be mistaken about?

I mean… in the abstract, yes. I know people can be mistaken about things. I’m not saying I’m incapable of being wrong. That would be arrogant, and I don’t want to come across that way.

But when I think about this specific situation, it’s hard for me to believe I’ve misunderstood the whole thing. I’m here because for almost two years I haven’t been able to shake the certainty that after that commission, a few people in the ensemble started doing things—small things, but consistent things—to quietly undermine my work. The schedule changes, the seating choices, the little comments in rehearsals that sound neutral if you isolate them, but in the room they felt pointed. Like they were shaping how people heard the piece, or how seriously they took me, without ever having to openly say anything.

And yes, they can show me emails or notes afterward that supposedly explain it. They can say, “This was logistics,” or “That was just a balance issue,” or “You’re reading too much into that.” I understand those explanations individually. I really do. But it’s the accumulation that makes it hard for me to say, “Oh, I just imagined all of that.”

So could I be mistaken? Technically, yes. I can say that. But emotionally—or honestly, practically—it doesn’t feel like a mistake. It feels like I noticed something that was meant to stay deniable.
Have you ever felt that your thoughts were being interfered with—like someone could put thoughts into your mind, take them out, or somehow know them directly?

No, not like that. I don’t think anyone is putting thoughts into my head or taking them out. That sounds… different from what I’m talking about.

I do sometimes wonder what people know or what they’ve picked up on, especially in a room where there’s tension, because you can tell when people are responding to something without saying it directly. But I don’t mean they can literally read my mind. I mean more like… people can infer things, or they know the history, or they’re reacting to the atmosphere.

My thoughts feel like my own. I may get stuck thinking about certain things, and I can go over them too much, but I don’t feel like someone else is controlling them or inserting them. So, no, I haven’t experienced that in the way you’re asking.
Have the people in the ensemble ever directly told you that they were not trying to undermine you?

Yes. A few times, directly enough. Not like some formal statement, but yes—people have said things like, “No one is trying to sabotage you,” or “You’re taking this personally,” or “These are just rehearsal logistics.” One person told me I was “reading intent into normal decisions,” which… I remember very clearly because it sounded reasonable on the surface, but it also felt like exactly the kind of thing someone would say if they wanted to keep it deniable.

And I know how that sounds. I do. If someone tells you, “We’re not trying to undermine you,” the normal response should probably be to accept it, or at least take it seriously. And I did try to consider it. But the problem is, those denials usually came after I pointed out one specific thing—like a schedule change, or a seating choice, or a comment in rehearsal that made my work seem less solid than it was. They would explain that one thing, sometimes even show an email or a note that made it look routine. But to me it didn’t explain why these things kept happening in the same direction, with the same few people involved, after that commission.

So yes, they’ve told me they weren’t trying to undermine me. I’m not saying nobody has denied it. It’s just that the denial doesn’t really touch the whole pattern. It answers the single incident in front of them, but not what I’ve been seeing for almost two years.
Other than this belief about the ensemble, have you had any other experiences that felt clearly out of touch with reality?

No… I don’t think so. Not in the way you mean, I don’t think I’ve had other things where I look back and think, “That was clearly not real,” or where other people are saying I’m completely disconnected from what’s happening.

It’s really this one situation with the ensemble. And I know I keep coming back to it, but that’s because it’s not just one odd moment to me. It’s been almost two years of feeling like, after that commission, a few people started doing these small, hard-to-prove things—moving things around in the schedule, making certain seating decisions, saying these little comments in rehearsals that could sound harmless if you wrote them down, but in context felt very deliberate. Like they were trying to weaken how my work was perceived without ever openly attacking it.

And the frustrating part is that when I bring up one example, they’ll have an explanation ready. They’ll show an email or a note and say, “See, this was just logistics,” or, “This was decided for balance,” or whatever. And I can understand those explanations in isolation. I’m not saying every single email is fake or anything like that. It’s more that the explanations don’t account for the whole pattern. They make each individual thing look normal, but they don’t explain why it kept lining up the same way, with the same people, after that commission.

But outside of that… no, I wouldn’t say I’ve had other experiences that felt clearly out of touch with reality. It’s this. This is the thing I can’t let go of.
Have you ever had a period when you heard voices speaking to you or about you?

No, I don’t think so. I’ve never had voices speaking to me, like from outside my head, or commenting on me in that way.

I mean, I can replay conversations in my mind a lot—especially rehearsals or things someone said that bothered me—and I’ll sort of hear the tone of it in memory, if that makes sense. Like remembering exactly how someone phrased something. But that’s not the same as hearing a voice when no one is there. It’s more like thinking about it too much afterward.

And I’ve been in rooms where I felt like people were talking around me, or that comments had a meaning aimed at me, but that’s different from actually hearing voices. I know the difference. So, no, I haven’t had a period where voices were speaking to me or about me.
Before this commission, had you ever been this certain that someone was deliberately trying to harm or undermine you?

No, not like this. I mean, I’ve had conflicts before, obviously—people disagreeing with me musically, or politics in school and ensembles, that kind of thing—but I don’t remember ever being this certain that someone was deliberately trying to harm my position or undermine my work.

This really started after I won the commission and was invited to conduct the premiere. That was about… a year and nine months ago now. And it’s strange, because before that I could usually tell myself, “Okay, maybe this person is being difficult,” or “Maybe I’m taking criticism too hard,” but after that point it felt different. It felt like things started lining up in a way that wasn’t just normal professional friction.

So before the commission, no—not with this level of certainty, and not for this long. This has been going on since then.
Since this started, have you had a period where you felt unusually energized and needed much less sleep than usual?

I’m not sure I’d describe it that way. I’ve definitely had stretches where I was wound up about the whole situation and stayed up too late thinking through things, replaying conversations, trying to make sense of what happened. But that feels different from being unusually energized or not needing sleep.

Like, if I slept badly, I’d feel it the next day. I’d be tired, distracted, maybe more on edge. It wasn’t like I suddenly had all this extra energy and could function on almost no sleep as if that were normal. It was more that my mind wouldn’t quiet down sometimes.

So… no, I don’t think I’ve had a period like that, not in the sense you’re asking.
Since this started, has your overall functioning at work or in daily life clearly declined?

I wouldn’t say it’s clearly declined overall, no. I mean, this issue with the ensemble has taken up a lot of mental space, more than I’d like, and I can get preoccupied with it, but outside of that specific situation I’m still functioning pretty normally.

I’m still meeting deadlines. I’m still composing, still keeping up with the work I need to get done. I run most mornings, which is kind of my way of keeping myself steady, and I haven’t just stopped doing that or fallen apart day-to-day. And at home, with my wife, things are basically steady. Not perfect, I mean, I’m sure she can tell when I’m tense about all of this, but it’s not like my whole life has collapsed.

So… no, I don’t think there’s been a clear overall decline. It’s more that this one area has become very consuming.
What is the strongest evidence you have that these ensemble members were deliberately trying to undermine you?

The strongest evidence is the pattern, honestly. I know that may sound less satisfying than, you know, one single email where someone says, “We’re trying to sabotage him,” but that’s not how people do things in a professional ensemble. It’s much quieter than that.

After I got the commission and was invited to conduct the premiere, things started changing in ways that seemed small individually but together were very hard to dismiss. Rehearsal schedules would shift in ways that made it harder for me to address certain passages properly, or I’d only find out about changes late. Seating choices would suddenly be different, and it would affect balance or make it harder for me to communicate with specific players. And then there were these little comments during rehearsal—nothing openly hostile, but phrased in a way that undercut my authority or made it seem like my choices were questionable.

And yes, they’ve shown me emails or notes that supposedly explain some of it. Like, “Oh, this was just a scheduling constraint,” or “We seated people this way because of availability,” or “That comment was taken out of context.” But the explanations feel too neat after the fact. They don’t account for how consistently the changes landed in a way that weakened my position.

So I guess the strongest evidence isn’t one dramatic thing. It’s that for almost two years, the same few people keep being connected to these schedule changes, seating decisions, and rehearsal comments, and somehow it always seems to make my work look less controlled or less prepared. At a certain point, it doesn’t feel accidental anymore.
Before this commission, did you often suspect that people were exploiting, deceiving, or trying to harm you, even in other parts of your life?

No, not really—not before this. I mean, I’m not saying I was naive or that I never had doubts about people’s motives, but I didn’t go around thinking people were trying to deceive me or harm me in some broad way.

This really started after I won the commission and then was invited to conduct the premiere. That was the turning point. Before that, I had the usual professional anxieties, I guess—wondering if people liked the work, whether a rehearsal went well, whether someone respected me—but not this kind of suspicion. The whole thing has been going on since then, so… about a year and nine months now.

It feels tied to that situation specifically, not like something I’ve always carried into every part of my life.
Even when you’re shown evidence that seems to contradict it, do you still remain certain that these ensemble members were deliberately undermining you?

Yes. I mean… yes, I do still feel certain, even when they show me things that are supposed to explain it away.

It’s not that I don’t understand what the emails or notes say. I can read them. I can see that on paper it looks like, “Oh, this schedule change was because of availability,” or “This seating decision was logistical,” or “That rehearsal comment wasn’t meant that way.” I get that. But those explanations don’t really touch the thing that makes me certain, which is the pattern over time.

After the commission, and especially once I was involved in conducting the premiere, it wasn’t just one odd rehearsal or one awkward comment. It was schedule changes, seating choices, little remarks in front of other people—small things, but always landing in a way that made my work harder or made me look less in control. And it kept happening with the same few people around it.

So when someone hands me an email afterward, I don’t feel reassured. It feels more like a clean explanation placed over something messier. Maybe that sounds stubborn, but I can’t shake the certainty that they were quietly undermining me. I’ve tried to talk myself out of it, but it still feels deliberate.

For almost two years now I haven’t been able to shake the feeling—well, not just a feeling, really—that after that commission, certain things started happening in a pattern: schedule changes that made my work harder to present properly, seating choices that affected how the piece came across, little comments in rehearsal that sounded harmless but seemed aimed at making people doubt the work or doubt me.

And I know how it sounds, because each individual thing can be explained. They’ll show an email or say, “No, that was decided for logistics,” or “That wasn’t about you,” or “That note was just about balance.” But taken together, it doesn’t feel accidental. It feels deliberate, just done in a way that’s easy to deny.

So, no, I wouldn’t say I’m convinced other people in general are trying to harm me. It’s this specific group, this specific situation, that I can’t let go of.

doctor.question: What is the strongest evidence you have that these ensemble members were deliberately trying to undermine you?

target_item.name: Delusions
target_item.manifestation: I’m here because for almost two years I’ve been unable to shake the certainty that after the commission, a few people in the ensemble started using schedule changes, seating choices, and little comments in rehearsals to quietly undermine my work, even when they show me emails or notes that supposedly explain it.

patient.answer:
The strongest evidence is the pattern, honestly. I know that may sound less satisfying than, you know, one single email where someone says, “We’re trying to sabotage him,” but that’s not how people do things in a professional ensemble. It’s much quieter than that.

After I got the commission and was invited to conduct the premiere, things started changing in ways that seemed small individually but together were very hard to dismiss. Rehearsal schedules would shift in ways that made it harder for me to address certain passages properly, or I’d only find out about changes late. Seating choices would suddenly be different, and it would affect balance or make it harder for me to communicate with specific players. And yes, they’ve shown me emails or notes that supposedly explain some of it. Like, “Oh, this was just a scheduling constraint,” or “We seated people this way because of availability,” or “That comment was taken out of context.” But the explanations feel too neat after the fact. They don’t account for how consistently the changes landed in a way that weakened my position.

So I guess the strongest evidence isn’t one dramatic thing. It’s that for almost two years, the same few people keep being connected to these schedule changes, seating decisions, and rehearsal comments, and somehow it always seems to make my work look less controlled or less prepared. At a certain point, it doesn’t feel accidental anymore.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient describes a persistent, circumscribed persecutory delusional belief lasting about 1 year and 9 months to 2 years, centered on specific ensemble members undermining his work. The belief remains fixed despite contradictory evidence and direct denials. There are no hallucinations, no thought insertion/withdrawal, no bizarre or impossible content, no disorganized speech, no negative symptoms, no manic syndrome, and no clear overall functional decline. This pattern is most consistent with persistent delusional disorder rather than schizophrenia-spectrum psychosis with broader symptoms or paranoid personality disorder, which is not supported by a longstanding premorbid pattern.
